query: Consider the following context: High-entropy alloy (HEA) multilayers represent a promising class of advanced coating materials due to their superior mechanical properties, corrosion resistance, and irradiation tolerance. However, the specific role of interface coherency on the creep behavior of HEA multilayers remains unclear. In that context, which material can be used for transition between diffusion-mediated and dislocation-mediated creep mechanisms, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a coherent tungsten-based interlayer in HEA multilayer coatings promotes a transition from diffusion-mediated to dislocation-mediated creep by reducing grain-boundary diffusion and providing an interface that assists dislocation nucleation and motion.
generation.material_initial_state: HEA multilayer coatings with typical incoherent or semi-coherent interfaces that under high temperature exhibit dominant diffusion-mediated creep.
generation.intervention: Incorporate a thin, tungsten or tungsten-based refractory HEA interlayer engineered to form highly coherent interfaces between adjacent HEA layers.
generation.conditions: Elevated temperature creep testing at intermediate to high stresses, where both diffusion and dislocation mechanisms may compete.
generation.structural_mediator: Coherent interfaces created by the tungsten interlayer that minimize lattice mismatch with the adjacent HEA layers.
generation.mechanism: The tungsten interlayer—with its high melting point and low diffusivity—reduces grain-boundary diffusion and acts as a barrier to atomic migration, thereby shifting the deformation mechanism from one dominated by atomic diffusion (diffusional creep) to one dominated by dislocation activity (dislocation creep). The coherent interface also provides favorable nucleation sites for dislocations, enhancing plasticity.
generation.predicted_outcome: Creep tests on multilayer samples with the tungsten interlayer will show a lower creep strain rate under the same stress and temperature conditions, and microstructural analysis will reveal increased dislocation density at the interfaces relative to samples without the interlayer.
generation.baseline: HEA multilayers without the tungsten interlayer, which typically exhibit a higher contribution of diffusion-mediated creep at elevated temperatures.
generation.boundary: The effect is expected to be significant in a specific range of temperatures and stresses where dislocation mobility is activated, while at very high temperatures diffusion may still dominate; the interlayer must also maintain its coherency and structural stability over the tested conditions.
generation.uncertainty: The exact temperature and stress thresholds at which the transition predominates, as well as the optimal thickness and composition of the tungsten interlayer, remain to be precisely determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HEA multilayer coatings: one set incorporating a thin tungsten (or W-based refractory HEA) interlayer designed to form coherent interfaces, and a control set without the interlayer. Subject both sets to identical elevated temperature creep tests under a range of stresses. Perform pre- and post-test microstructural characterization using TEM to assess dislocation density, interface coherency, and evidence of diffusional versus dislocation creep mechanisms.
measurements: Creep strain rate as a function of temperature and stress
Dislocation density and interface structure (via TEM)
Grain boundary diffusion markers (e.g., secondary ion mass spectrometry if applicable)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the samples with the tungsten interlayer show no statistically significant decrease in creep strain rate or no increase in dislocation activity compared to control samples—i.e., if the creep mechanism remains dominantly diffusional under the tested conditions—the hypothesis is falsified.

Research has proved that RHEAs have excellent mechanical properties at high temperatures, even surpassing the widely used nickel-based alloy [ [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] ]. Even though there was an increase in the grain size during He implantation, the material preserved its nano-crystallinity and showed only approximately 10 nm change in grain size after ~8.45 at.% He implantation. The previously studied quaternary W-Ta-Cr-V RHEA demonstrated a similar thermal stability regarding grain morphology [22] . One of the properties that distinguishes this quinary W-Ta-Cr-V-Hf RHEA from the previously studied RHEAs is the grain refinement observed during dual-beam irradiation. Abstract Conventional material processing approaches often achieve strengthening of materials at the cost of reduced ductility. Here, we show that high-pressure and high-temperature (HPHT) treatment can help overcome the strength-ductility trade-off in structural materials. We report an initially strong-yet-brittle eutectic high entropy alloy simultaneously doubling its strength to 1150 MPa and its tensile ductility to 36% after the HPHT treatment. Such strength-ductility synergy is attributed to the HPHT-induced formation of a hierarchically patterned microstructure with coherent interfaces, which promotes multiple deformation mechanisms, including dislocations, stacking faults, microbands and deformation twins, at multiple length scales. More importantly, the HPHT-induced microstructure helps relieve stress concentration at the interfaces, thereby arresting interfacial cracking commonly observed in traditional eutectic high entropy alloys. These findings suggest a new direction of research in employing HPHT techniques to help develop next generation structural materials. Subject terms: Metals and alloys, Mechanical properties, Mechanical engineering
